research.title: Optical imaging for liver transplantation
research.affiliation: Tang Biophotonic Imaging Lab · CURE Fellowship
research.summary: Can high-resolution optical imaging help characterize bile duct tissue before liver transplantation?
research.context: Bile duct injury can complicate liver transplantation. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) captures cross-sectional images of tissue, giving the research team a way to study microstructural changes before comparing them with reference methods.
research.contribution: I processed donor bile duct OCT scans, annotated tissue boundaries, and extracted image features. I standardized acquisition metadata, compared adjacent scans, and flagged ambiguous boundaries for review.
research.outcome: The team studied 20 donor bile ducts ex vivo and compared OCT findings with confocal microscopy and histology. I presented my work at the CURE Summer Research Symposium and the OU UReCA Showcase. The team’s conference abstract appeared in the 2025 END2CANCER program.
research.limit: The study evaluated tissue ex vivo. A transplant viability decision rule would require prospective clinical validation.

research.title: Model quantization for portable imaging
research.affiliation: INQUIRE Lab · Provost’s Summer UReCA Fellowship
research.summary: How does model compression change the trade-off between accuracy, inference time, and file size on a CPU?
research.context: For resource-constrained imaging systems, a smaller model can be attractive. Image classification on a held-out public microscopy dataset provided a controlled setting to measure how compression affected the full set of deployment metrics.
research.contribution: I built a reusable Python preprocessing pipeline for public NIH/NLM malaria cell images and benchmarked two TensorFlow Lite classifier variants. I held the split fixed, checked for file-path overlap, and used confusion matrices to examine errors.
research.outcome: I prepared the 2026 UReCA fellowship poster on quantization for portable biomedical imaging. The benchmark measured classification accuracy, model footprint, and inference time under matched conditions.
research.limit: This was a dataset and CPU benchmark. Deployment latency, power use, and clinical performance would require additional testing.

workflow.title: How the benchmark controls the comparison
steps: Use the same held-out microscopy images for both models.
Benchmark the full-precision and quantized variants on one CPU thread.
Check accuracy, model size, and inference time together.
workflow.caption: Holding inputs and runtime conditions steady makes the two TensorFlow Lite variants directly comparable.

research.title: Controlled evaluation of edge inference
research.summary: How can matched baselines and realistic evaluation splits isolate where a model architecture helps?
research.context: When evaluating spiking architectures, preprocessing choices and differences in decision rules can obscure which component affects performance. An ECG experiment poses a related challenge because samples from the same patient can be correlated.
research.contribution: I led the design and evaluation of a spoken-action benchmark with matched controls, applying calibration, risk–coverage analysis, and paired resampling. I also contributed to ECG edge-inference research using patient-grouped recordings and simulated inference deadlines.
research.outcome: The spoken-action and ECG work are research projects. My published IEEE coauthorship is a separate comparative study of neuromorphic hardware for edge intelligence.
research.limit: These evaluations address specific datasets and timing assumptions. Performance in prospective or hardware-in-the-loop settings requires separate evaluation.

workflow.title: How the spoken-action evaluation isolates the model
steps: Compare models under the same evaluation setup.
Check which predictions remain when the decision threshold changes.
workflow.caption: The workflow separates the model comparison from decisions about confidence and coverage.

engineering.title: Analog spiking-neuron hardware
engineering.summary: Design, simulation, and bench testing of a Zener-clamped analog spiking-neuron circuit.
engineering.context: Analog spiking circuits offer a hardware path for event-based computation. My work on the FUGAZ circuit studied how measured firing behavior compares with simulation and supported a fellowship proposal for low-power neuroprosthetic applications.
engineering.contribution: I designed and assembled the circuit board, bench-tested it with an oscilloscope and function generator, and compared the measured waveforms with NGSpice and COMSOL simulations. I analyzed spike trains in Python and MATLAB.
engineering.outcome: I used bench and simulation comparisons to evaluate the prototype and developed an ART InTRO proposal to adapt the design for low-power neuroprosthetics.
engineering.limit: The circuit is research hardware. The proposed application would require device-level testing and validation.

workflow.title: From circuit design to bench evaluation
steps: Drive the circuit with a function generator and record waveforms on an oscilloscope.
Review measured spike trains against NGSpice and COMSOL simulations.
workflow.caption: The comparison was performed on research hardware in the lab.

engineering.title: Wearable stretch-sensor prototype
engineering.summary: A wearable sensing prototype for exploring limb circumference monitoring in lymphedema.
engineering.context: The team explored using a stretch sensor to detect changes in circumference, which required conditioning a small resistance change for readout on a microcontroller.
engineering.contribution: I built the team’s Wheatstone-bridge sensor circuit and used Arduino Uno serial voltage readings to troubleshoot bridge imbalance.
engineering.outcome: Serial readouts provided a way to inspect the electrical response and investigate imbalance as the team developed the prototype.
engineering.limit: The work was a course prototype. Sensor calibration and clinical measurement accuracy would require further validation.

engineering.title: Adaptive toothbrush holder
engineering.summary: Requirements, concept selection, and prototype fit checks for an assistive oral-care device.
engineering.context: The capstone team explored an adaptive toothbrush holder, with design decisions shaped by fit, adjustability, and ease of use.
engineering.contribution: I documented requirements, compared three concepts with a weighted decision matrix, and used fit checks to inform a crown-strap revision. I applied standards knowledge while reviewing design choices.
engineering.outcome: The team iterated the prototype following fit checks. The revised strap addressed an issue identified during that process.
engineering.limit: Fit checks informed development. Formal device verification, compliance testing, and user validation would be separate steps.
